runs.advice_text:
De-escalating an upset stakeholder
- Let them finish; interrupting increases frustration.
- Name the emotion and the impact before explaining causes.
- Keep explanations short and non-technical, then pivot to the plan.

Apologizing with ownership
- Apologize for the specific impact, not 'any inconvenience'.
- Avoid shifting blame to other teams, vendors, or the client.
- Pair the apology with what is changing so it doesn't happen again.

Closing with clear commitments
- A good close names the action, the owner, and the date.
- Ask the other person to restate the agreement, or restate it yourself and confirm.
- Offer a check-in point so the commitment has a natural follow-up.

transcript.content: I'm an account manager at a software company. A bug in our integration with a client's scheduling system pushed their patient-portal launch back a week, after they'd already told about 3,000 patients it would go live Monday. Their Director of Operations, Marcus, is upset and calling me. Can you role-play Marcus so I can practice? Stay in character until I say 'end role-play'. Start with Marcus's first line.

I just got off the phone with our support team. We told 3,000 patients the portal would be live today, and now you’re telling us it’s delayed a week because of an integration bug? How did this happen—and what are you going to do about it?
You're right to be upset, and I'm sorry. This one's on us: a bug in our integration with your scheduling system was caught in final testing and pushed your launch.

Caught in final testing? So this wasn’t discovered until the last minute, after we’d already told thousands of patients? I need to understand why your checks didn’t catch it sooner—and I need a concrete plan for what happens now, not just an apology.
Our engineers found the root cause and expect the fix verified by Thursday. I'd like to show you a working demo on staging Friday.

That’s a start, but “expect” isn’t a commitment—and a staging demo doesn’t undo the disruption to our patients or staff. What happens if the fix isn’t verified Thursday? And what can you give us today to help manage the message to patients who were expecting the portal this morning?
I'll send you a written summary today by 5 p.m. that you can forward to your CEO. Can we check in Wednesday at 10?

I can make Wednesday at 10, but that’s before your Thursday verification target. What will we review then—actual test results, a revised timeline, or just another status update? And I still need something today we can use for patients. Can your team provide approved patient-facing language, plus a clear point of contact if staff get questions?
For the go/no-go, I'll own that decision with our engineering lead, and if Thursday's verification fails we'll tell you the same day and agree a new date together before anything goes to patients.

Good—you owning the go/no-go is important. But I don’t want to wait until Thursday to learn we’re in trouble. Can you give us an update Wednesday with the test progress and any risks, and send the patient-facing language and staff contact today? Also, who from your side will be accountable for keeping us informed?
End role-play. Give me feedback on how I handled it and what I should do differently next time.

You handled the conversation with accountability and a calm tone. You acknowledged the impact without getting defensive, then moved toward concrete next steps. That helped keep Marcus focused on resolving the issue rather than escalating the conflict.

### What worked well
- **You took responsibility:** “This one’s on us” was direct and avoided blame-shifting.
- **You shared specific progress:** Naming the root cause and a Thursday verification target gave Marcus something tangible.
- **You offered a follow-up deliverable:** A written summary with a firm deadline was useful.
- **You clarified decision ownership:** Saying you’d own the go/no-go with engineering, and that you wouldn’t announce a new date without agreement, addressed trust and control.

### What to improve
- **Acknowledge the patient and operational impact more explicitly.** The 3,000 patients and the staff who must respond to them are central. You could say: “I understand you’ve already set expectations with roughly 3,000 patients, and this puts your team in a difficult position.”
- **Don’t let the immediate need go unanswered.** Marcus twice asked for patient-facing language and a staff contact. Your replies didn’t address those requests. Commit to a specific action and deadline—or explain what you need to produce it.
- **Make the technical plan more measurable.** “Expect the fix verified by Thursday” is appropriately cautious, but say what verification includes, who is doing it, and when you’ll report progress. Avoid implying a date is firm before the evidence is in.
- **Build in an earlier warning point.** Marcus specifically wanted an update before Thursday. Offer a Wednesday checkpoint with test progress, risks, and a clear escalation path.
- **Be precise about the written summary.** A CEO-forwardable summary is useful, but it shouldn’t replace the patient communication Marcus needs. Consider committing to both separately.

### A stronger response could sound like this
> “I understand you’ve already told about 3,000 patients the portal would be available today, and this creates real work for your staff as well as a loss of confidence. I’ll send you two items by 5 p.m. today: a concise patient-facing delay notice for your review and a written incident summary with the cause, impact, owners, and recovery plan. I’ll also name a single contact for your team. On Wednesday at 10, we’ll review test progress and risks—not just provide a status update. If verification is at risk, I’ll tell you immediately rather than waiting until Thursday. I’ll own coordinating the go/no-go with our engineering lead, and we’ll agree on any new launch date together before it’s communicated.”

The main opportunity is to pair your apology and technical plan with immediate help for the people affected—and to answer every direct request before moving to the next topic.

transcript.content: I'm an account manager at a software company. A bug in our integration with a client's scheduling system pushed their patient-portal launch back a week, after they'd already told about 3,000 patients it would go live Monday. Their Director of Operations, Marcus, is upset and calling me. Can you role-play Marcus so I can practice? Stay in character until I say 'end role-play'. Start with Marcus's first line.
I’ve got about 3,000 patients expecting the portal to go live today, and now I’m hearing it’s delayed a week because of an integration bug. What happened—and what are you going to do about it?
You're right to be upset, and I'm sorry. This one's on us: a bug in our integration with your scheduling system was caught in final testing and pushed your launch.

You’re saying it was caught in final testing—but why wasn’t this identified sooner, before we told patients Monday? And what can you tell me right now about the new launch date and how you’ll help us communicate this to those 3,000 patients?
Our engineers found the root cause and expect the fix verified by Thursday. I'd like to show you a working demo on staging Friday.

“Expect” isn’t a firm date, and a demo on Friday doesn’t give us much time to decide what to tell patients. What happens if the fix doesn’t pass verification Thursday? I need a clear go/no-go date, a contingency plan, and someone accountable for keeping my team updated.
I'll send you a written summary today by 5 p.m. that you can forward to your CEO. Can we check in Wednesday at 10?

A written summary for my CEO is useful, but it doesn’t answer what I need for the patients or my operations team. And Wednesday at 10 is before your Thursday verification—what exactly will we know by then? I need a patient communication plan, a clear decision point, and a named person who’ll keep us updated if anything changes.
For the go/no-go, I'll own that decision with our engineering lead, and if Thursday's verification fails we'll tell you the same day and agree a new date together before anything goes to patients.

That’s a start, but I’m still uncomfortable with “agree a new date together” after another failure. We’ve already lost credibility with patients once. What safeguards will you put in place before we announce anything else, and can you give me a patient-facing message today that my team can review? Also, who specifically is my day-to-day contact?
End role-play. Give me feedback on how I handled it and what I should do differently next time.

You handled the opening well: you acknowledged the impact, apologized clearly, and accepted responsibility without making excuses. You also offered a written update and proposed a check-in, which showed initiative.

Where you can improve:

- **Address the patient impact directly.** Marcus repeatedly asked how to communicate with the 3,000 patients. Offer to draft a patient-facing message and help coordinate delivery—not just an internal summary.
- **Make the plan concrete.** “Expect the fix verified by Thursday” sounded uncertain, while the proposed Wednesday check-in came before that milestone. Set specific checkpoints, explain what will be known at each one, and give a firm go/no-go time.
- **Clarify ownership.** You said you would own the decision with engineering, but didn’t name a day-to-day contact or explain who would send updates. Assign one accountable person and a clear update cadence.
- **Define safeguards and contingencies.** If verification fails, say what happens next: who investigates, when Marcus hears from you, what criteria must pass before rescheduling, and how you’ll avoid announcing another date prematurely.
- **Avoid putting the burden back on the client.** “Agree a new date together” is collaborative, but Marcus needs you to bring a credible recommendation and evidence—not ask him to solve the problem.

A stronger response to his last concern might be:

> “I’ll send you a draft patient message today for your review, along with the verification criteria and a go/no-go time for Thursday. I’ll be your day-to-day contact and will update you at [specific times], even if there’s no change. We won’t recommend a new launch date until the fix passes the agreed checks, including an end-to-end scheduling test. If it fails, I’ll call you the same day with the findings, recovery plan, and next decision point.”

The main opportunity is to move from apology and reassurance to a **specific recovery plan** that addresses patients, accountability, decision timing, and prevention of another premature launch announcement.

You're right to be upset, and I'm sorry. This one's on us: a bug in our integration with your scheduling system was caught in final testing and pushed your launch.

Caught in final testing? So this wasn’t even resolved before we told patients Monday was the launch date? I need more than an apology. What exactly failed, when will it be fixed, and what are you doing to help us communicate this change to 3,000 patients?
Our engineers found the root cause and expect the fix verified by Thursday. I'd like to show you a working demo on staging Friday.

What’s the earliest realistic launch date after that demo, and what happens if the fix doesn’t pass verification on Thursday? Also, can you help us with a clear message to patients today?
I'll send you a written summary today by 5 p.m. that you can forward to your CEO. Can we check in Wednesday at 10?

A summary for my CEO is useful, but it doesn’t address the patients who are expecting this on Monday. I need a patient-facing message today, plus a concrete plan with owners and dates—not just a check-in. And Wednesday at 10 is too late if verification is Thursday. Can we meet tomorrow, and can you tell me who will be accountable for the fix and the launch decision?
For the go/no-go, I'll own that decision with our engineering lead, and if Thursday's verification fails we'll tell you the same day and agree a new date together before anything goes to patients.

I appreciate you taking ownership, but I need the specifics in writing: what “verification” includes, who the engineering lead is, and what time Thursday you’ll give us the result. We can agree on a new date together, but I don’t want another patient announcement until we’ve confirmed the integration works end to end. Who’s drafting the patient message, and when will I have it?
End role-play. Give me feedback on how I handled it and what I should do differently next time.

You handled the conversation well overall: you acknowledged the impact, took responsibility, and offered a next step rather than becoming defensive. You also gave Marcus clear ownership of the go/no-go decision and committed to same-day communication if verification fails.

What worked:
- **Direct accountability:** “This one’s on us” avoided blaming the client or the scheduling system.
- **A specific update:** You shared the root cause was found and gave a target for verification and a staging demo.
- **Ownership and contingency:** You said you’d own the launch decision and would report a failed verification the same day.

What to improve:
- **Address the patient impact immediately.** Marcus’s biggest concern was the 3,000 patients who had already been told Monday. Offer to help draft a patient-facing notice and agree on when it will go out.
- **Don’t let the first proposed meeting replace urgent coordination.** Wednesday was too late when verification was Thursday. Acknowledge that and propose a nearer check-in with a specific time.
- **Make the timeline more decision-ready.** Distinguish the fix being completed, verification passing, the staging demo, and the earliest responsible launch date. Avoid implying that a Friday demo necessarily means the portal can launch immediately.
- **Define the contingency before it happens.** Say what will be tested, who will confirm it, when Marcus will hear the result, and what the next step is if it fails.

You're right to be upset, and I'm sorry. This one's on us: a bug in our integration with your scheduling system was caught in final testing and pushed your launch.

Our engineers found the root cause and expect the fix verified by Thursday. I'd like to show you a working demo on staging Friday.

Thursday verification and a Friday demo are a start, but that still leaves patients and my front desk in limbo. What exactly will you do to support us through the delay, and when will I have the written plan?
I'll send you a written summary today by 5 p.m. that you can forward to your CEO. Can we check in Wednesday at 10?

Good—send it by 5, with the patient-facing message, front-desk guidance, and clear owners and checkpoints through Thursday’s verification and Friday’s demo. Wednesday at 10 works. I also need to know what you’re offering to make this right for the disruption we’ve caused.
For the go/no-go, I'll own that decision with our engineering lead, and if Thursday's verification fails we'll tell you the same day and agree a new date together before anything goes to patients.

That’s the kind of accountability I need. Put that go/no-go ownership and same-day escalation in the written plan, along with the patient and front-desk support. I still need an answer on how you’ll make this right for the disruption.
